questions.q: Why is this capstone's Power Query cleanup lighter than Chapter 3's general lessons?
options: AdventureWorksDW2014 is a well-built data warehouse, so heavier techniques like unpivoting or merging queries aren't needed here
Power Query doesn't work with SQL Server data at all
This project skips Power Query entirely
Cleanup is never needed for any warehouse-sourced data
questions.explain: The source data is already well-structured, so the real work here is trimming, renaming, and type-checking — not the deeper reshaping techniques Chapter 3 covered for messier sources.

questions.q: What is the correct approach to the columns Lesson 85 deliberately over-imported?
options: Now that you can see the actual data, decide for real which extras to remove and which to keep
Leave every single column exactly as imported, forever
Remove all extra columns automatically without review
Import even more columns to be extra safe
questions.explain: Lesson 85's advice to over-import was specifically so this lesson could make an informed decision — now that the data is visible, trim what's genuinely unneeded.

questions.q: What should renaming or removing a column NEVER do to a table?
options: Change its row count
Change its column names
Change its data types
Change its Applied Steps
questions.explain: Renaming and removing columns shouldn't affect row count. A changed row count after cleanup signals an unintended filter step, not a rename or column removal.

questions.q: What is a common data-type quirk worth double-checking on the fact tables in this capstone?
options: That OrderDate, DueDate, and ShipDate actually loaded as Date type, not text
That every numeric column loaded as a string
That every column loaded as Date type
That the table names loaded correctly
questions.explain: Warehouse date columns sometimes load with an unexpected type — verifying OrderDate/DueDate/ShipDate are genuinely Date type (not text) avoids downstream DAX and relationship problems.

options: Commits every Power Query transformation step back into the semantic model, the same schema-refresh mechanic covered in Lesson 75
Publishes the report directly to the Power BI service
Deletes all Applied Steps without saving them
Only applies renames, not column removals
questions.explain: Close & Apply re-reads the current structure and applies every Power Query step in order — it's the Desktop-side schema refresh Lesson 75 described as the fix for structural changes.
